posts.title: LLM-in-SQL: What Snowflake Cortex Actually Changes for Analytics Teams
posts.excerpt: Snowflake Cortex lets you call large language models with a single SQL function. Here is where that genuinely helps, where it does not, and how to ship it without surprising your finance team.
posts.body:
## The pitch, minus the hype

Snowflake Cortex exposes large language models as SQL functions you call inside the warehouse. No model hosting, no separate inference cluster, no data leaving your Snowflake account. For teams that already live in SQL, that removes most of the operational friction that has historically kept LLMs in the "someday" column.

The interesting part is not that you *can* call a model from SQL. It is that the model now sits next to your governed data, inheriting the same roles, masking policies, and audit trail you already trust.

## The functions you will actually use

Most real work concentrates on a handful of functions:

- `AI_COMPLETE` (formerly `COMPLETE`) — general prompting against a chosen model
- `AI_CLASSIFY` — bucket text into categories you define
- `AI_FILTER` — boolean predicate over unstructured text, usable in a `WHERE` clause
- `AI_AGG` — summarise across many rows without hitting context limits
- `EXTRACT_ANSWER` and `SENTIMENT` — narrow, cheap, predictable

A classification job that used to be a Python service becomes one statement:

```sql
SELECT
  ticket_id,
  AI_CLASSIFY(
    body,
    ['billing', 'bug', 'feature_request', 'churn_risk']
  ):labels[0]::string AS category
FROM support_tickets
WHERE created_at >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_DATE());
```

That result is a governed table. You can join it, schedule it in a task, and grant it like anything else.

## Where Cortex earns its keep

The strongest use cases share a shape: high-volume, unstructured text that needs structure applied to it.

- **Support and CRM enrichment** — categorising tickets, extracting product names, scoring sentiment at scale.
- **Document triage** — classifying and routing inbound PDFs, contracts, claims.
- **Analyst acceleration** — `AI_AGG` to summarise thousands of survey responses into themes.
- **Cortex Analyst** — natural-language questions answered against a governed semantic model, which is a meaningfully different thing from a generic chatbot because the model only sees your defined metrics and dimensions.

## Where it does not belong

Be honest with stakeholders about the limits:

- **Anything requiring sub-second latency per request.** Cortex is throughput-friendly, not a real-time inference endpoint for a customer-facing app.
- **Deterministic financial calculations.** Do not ask a model to compute revenue. Compute it in SQL; use the model to explain or narrate.
- **Tasks where a cheap rules engine already works.** A regex beats a model for extracting a well-formed order number.

## The cost conversation, before finance has it for you

Cortex bills by tokens consumed, surfaced as credits. The trap is running an `AI_COMPLETE` across a 50-million-row table in a backfill and discovering the bill on Monday. Guardrails we put in place on every engagement:

- Process **incremental slices**, not full-table scans, using streams and tasks.
- Pick the **smallest model that passes evaluation**. The largest model is rarely worth 5x the cost for classification.
- Track spend with `CORTEX_FUNCTIONS_USAGE_HISTORY` and put a **resource monitor** on the warehouse running the jobs.
- Cache results. If the input text has not changed, do not re-infer.

```sql
SELECT model_name,
       SUM(token_credits) AS credits
FROM snowflake.account_usage.cortex_functions_usage_history
WHERE start_time >= DATEADD(day, -30, CURRENT_DATE())
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
```

## Governance is the actual advantage

The reason we recommend Cortex over a bolt-on LLM API for warehouse-resident workloads is rarely the model quality. It is that the data never leaves the security boundary you have already audited. Masking policies still apply. Row access policies still apply. The query shows up in `QUERY_HISTORY`. For regulated clients in financial services and healthcare across the Americas, that single property collapses a months-long data-residency review into a much shorter one.

## How to start without a big-bang project

1. Pick one high-volume text classification or extraction task with a clear, measurable baseline.
2. Build a small **evaluation set** of 100-200 hand-labelled examples. This is non-negotiable — it is how you choose a model and prove value.
3. Run two models against it, compare accuracy and cost, and pick the cheaper one that clears your bar.
4. Productionise as a scheduled task on an incremental stream, with a resource monitor.
5. Review accuracy monthly. Models and prompts drift.

Cortex does not replace your data platform strategy. It removes the operational excuse for not putting LLMs to work on the text you already own. Start narrow, measure honestly, and let the governed-data advantage do the heavy lifting.

posts.title: Earn the Right to Do AI: Why Data Strategy Comes First
posts.excerpt: Most failed AI projects are not AI problems — they are data problems wearing a costume. Here is the sequence that actually gets a model into production.
posts.body:
## The uncomfortable pattern

We are brought in to "do AI" more often than anything else. Within the first two weeks, on roughly four out of five engagements, the conversation quietly shifts. The model is the easy part. The hard part is that nobody can agree what a "customer" is, the revenue figure differs across three dashboards, and the data the model needs is locked in a system the owning team will not grant access to.

AI does not fix a broken data foundation. It amplifies it. A model trained on inconsistent definitions produces confident, inconsistent answers — which is worse than no answer, because people act on it.

## What "data strategy" actually means here

It is not a 40-page document. It is a small number of decisions made deliberately rather than by accident:

- **What questions the business is actually trying to answer**, ranked by value.
- **Which data those questions require**, and who owns it.
- **A single source of truth** for the metrics that matter, with agreed definitions.
- **Who is allowed to see what**, encoded as policy, not tribal knowledge.
- **How data moves** from source to decision, and who is accountable at each step.

If you cannot answer those five, you are not ready for AI. You are ready to *get* ready, which is valuable and far cheaper than a failed model.

## The maturity ladder

We assess clients against a simple progression. You cannot skip rungs.

1. **Accessible** — the data exists somewhere you can query it. Surprisingly, many organisations fail here.
2. **Trusted** — definitions are agreed and tested. Revenue means the same thing everywhere.
3. **Governed** — access is controlled by policy, and you can prove who saw what.
4. **Modelled** — a semantic layer exposes business concepts, not raw tables.
5. **Activated** — data feeds decisions, products, and now models.

AI lives on rung five. Teams that try to jump from rung two straight to AI build impressive demos that never survive contact with production.

## A concrete first 90 days

For a client who wants AI but is honestly on rung two, the sequence that works:

- **Weeks 1-3: Decision inventory.** Interview the people who make money decisions. Catalogue the questions they ask and the data those questions need. Rank by value and feasibility.
- **Weeks 4-7: Source of truth.** Pick the top three metrics. Reconcile their definitions. Build them once, correctly, in a governed layer (we typically use dbt on Snowflake). Deprecate the conflicting versions.
- **Weeks 8-10: Governance baseline.** Implement role-based access, masking on sensitive columns, and an audit trail. This is what unlocks the regulated-data use cases later.
- **Weeks 11-13: One activated use case.** Now pick a single AI or advanced-analytics use case sitting on top of the trusted, governed foundation. Ship it.

Notice that the AI shows up in the last fortnight. By then it is almost boring, because the hard problems are solved.

## How to tell leadership without sounding obstructive

The instinct when an executive says "I want AI" is to either say yes immediately or to explain why it is hard. Both fail. The framing that works:

> "We can have an AI use case in production in a quarter. The first six weeks make it trustworthy, the last six make it intelligent. If we skip the first six, we will ship something in three weeks that we will spend the next year apologising for."

Executives understand sequencing. They do not want to fund the apology year.

## The signals you are ready

You are genuinely ready to invest in AI when:

- A new analyst can find the right table without asking three people.
- Two dashboards built by two teams show the same number for the same metric.
- You can answer "who accessed this customer's data last month" in minutes.
- There is a named owner for every critical dataset.

None of those require AI. All of them make AI work. That is the whole point: data strategy is not the thing you do *instead* of AI. It is the thing that makes AI stop being a science project and start being infrastructure.

posts.title: Migrating Off Teradata, Netezza, and On-Prem Oracle: A Field Guide to Snowflake
posts.excerpt: A pragmatic playbook for moving a legacy data warehouse to Snowflake without a two-year death march or a big-bang cutover that nobody trusts.
posts.body:
## Why these migrations stall

Legacy warehouse migrations rarely fail on technology. They fail on scope. A team sets out to "migrate the warehouse," discovers 4,000 stored procedures and 900 reports of unknown ownership, and either freezes or attempts a big-bang rewrite that slips for eighteen months. The way through is ruthless prioritisation and a parallel-run discipline.

## Step one: inventory and triage, not migrate

Before moving anything, build a real inventory:

- **Tables and their actual usage.** Query the source system's access logs. On most platforms, 60-80% of objects have not been touched in a year. You do not migrate those — you archive them.
- **Reports and dashboards, by last-run date and audience.** Half are abandoned.
- **ETL jobs and stored procedures**, grouped by the data products they feed.
- **Downstream consumers.** Who breaks if a table changes?

Triage into three buckets: **migrate as-is**, **rebuild better**, and **retire**. The retire bucket is your single biggest source of saved time. Defending it to stakeholders is the political work of the project.

## Step two: pick a pattern

There are three credible approaches.

- **Lift-and-shift then optimise.** Replicate structures into Snowflake, repoint, then refactor. Fastest to cutover, but you carry forward legacy design sins (and legacy costs) until you circle back — and teams rarely circle back.
- **Re-architect on the way.** Redesign the model for Snowflake's strengths — separate storage and compute, ELT instead of ETL, semi-structured `VARIANT` columns instead of shredding JSON on ingest. Slower start, far better destination.
- **Hybrid.** Lift-and-shift the stable, well-understood subject areas; re-architect the painful ones. This is what we recommend most often.

## Step three: handle the SQL dialect honestly

The code conversion is where optimism dies. Teradata `QUALIFY`, Oracle `CONNECT BY`, proprietary date functions, and implicit type coercions all need attention. Automated converters get you 70-85% of the way. The last 15% is where correctness bugs hide.

The rule we enforce: **a converted query is not done until it produces identical output to the source on the same input.** That requires a parallel run.

## Step four: parallel run is the whole game

For a defined window — usually 4 to 8 weeks per subject area — both systems run side by side and you reconcile output automatically.

```sql
-- Row-count and checksum reconciliation per critical table
SELECT 'orders_fact' AS table_name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy_repl.orders_fact) AS legacy_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.orders_fact)   AS snowflake_rows,
       (SELECT SUM(HASH(order_id, amount, status))
          FROM legacy_repl.orders_fact)               AS legacy_hash,
       (SELECT SUM(HASH(order_id, amount, status))
          FROM analytics.orders_fact)                 AS snowflake_hash;
```

When counts and hashes match across the critical tables for a full cycle, that subject area is cleared for cutover. This is what lets you tell a sceptical CFO the numbers are right — you can prove it, not assert it.

## Step five: cut over by subject area

Never big-bang. Cut over one subject area at a time — finance first if you want credibility, or a low-risk domain first if you want a rehearsal. Keep the legacy read path available for a rollback window. Communicate each cutover to downstream consumers individually; "the warehouse is moving" is not a communication, it is a rumour.

## What changes for the team

Snowflake is not Oracle with a new logo. The operating model shifts:

- **Compute is elastic and billed by the second.** This is a benefit and a liability. Idle warehouses cost nothing; runaway ones cost a lot. Resource monitors and auto-suspend become day-one hygiene.
- **You stop pre-aggregating defensively.** Much of the legacy summary-table sprawl existed to dodge expensive scans. Snowflake's architecture removes the need; resist the urge to recreate it.
- **ETL becomes ELT.** Land raw, transform in-warehouse with dbt. The transformation logic becomes version-controlled, tested code instead of opaque procedures.

## A realistic timeline

For a mid-sized warehouse — a few hundred active tables, a couple of thousand reports — a well-run migration lands in **6 to 9 months** with the hybrid approach. The variance is almost entirely down to two things: how aggressively you retire, and how clean the source data lineage is. Teams that skip the inventory phase to "save time" reliably spend that time threefold during reconciliation.

The goal is not just a new platform. It is arriving on Snowflake with a model worth keeping, costs under control, and stakeholders who trust the numbers because you showed them the reconciliation.

posts.title: Power BI vs ThoughtSpot vs Sigma: Choosing a BI Tool Without Regret
posts.excerpt: Three good tools, three different bets about who uses analytics and how. A consultant's decision framework for picking the one your organisation will not outgrow in a year.
posts.body:
## Stop comparing features

Feature matrices are how BI selections go wrong. Every modern tool has dashboards, drill-downs, scheduling, and an AI assistant on the roadmap. The features converge; the *philosophy* does not. The right question is not "which has more features" but "which tool's worldview matches how my organisation actually makes decisions."

We deploy all three regularly. Here is the honest shape of each.

## Power BI: the corporate standard

Power BI wins on gravity. If you are a Microsoft shop with Office 365, Azure AD, and Teams, it slots in with near-zero friction and the per-user licensing is hard to beat on cost.

- **Strengths:** ubiquitous, cheap at scale, deep formatting control, enormous talent pool, strong governance via Fabric and workspaces.
- **Watch out for:** DAX has a steep, idiosyncratic learning curve; the desktop-authoring model can create report sprawl; performance tuning on large models is a specialist skill; the Mac story is weak.
- **Best when:** you have a central BI team producing governed reports for a broad audience, and Microsoft is already your backbone.

## ThoughtSpot: search and AI-first

ThoughtSpot bets that business users want to *ask questions*, not consume pre-built dashboards. You type or speak a question and it generates the answer. Its Spotter AI agent leans hard into natural-language analytics.

- **Strengths:** genuine self-service for non-technical users, excellent natural-language querying, strong on a well-modelled cloud warehouse, good embedded story.
- **Watch out for:** the search experience is only as good as the underlying data model — garbage model, garbage answers; pricing skews higher; pixel-perfect formatting is not its strength.
- **Best when:** you have a trustworthy semantic model already, and a population of curious business users you want to take off the report-request queue.

## Sigma: spreadsheet UX on the warehouse

Sigma's insight is that millions of analysts are fluent in spreadsheets and terrified of SQL. It gives them a spreadsheet interface that runs live against the cloud warehouse — no extracts, no row limits.

- **Strengths:** flattest learning curve for Excel-native analysts, live warehouse queries (no stale extracts), genuinely good for collaborative ad-hoc analysis, strong write-back and input-table features.
- **Watch out for:** consumption-based warehouse cost can surprise you if users run wild; younger ecosystem than Power BI; needs a performant warehouse underneath.
- **Best when:** your analysts live in spreadsheets, you are already on Snowflake or BigQuery, and you want ad-hoc analysis without an extract layer.

## The decision framework

Answer these in order. The first one that gives a clear signal usually decides it.

1. **Who is the primary user?** Central BI team building for consumers → Power BI. Curious business users asking questions → ThoughtSpot. Spreadsheet-fluent analysts doing ad-hoc work → Sigma.
2. **What is your data foundation?** ThoughtSpot and Sigma assume a clean, performant cloud warehouse and a semantic model. If you do not have that yet, fix it first — or default to Power BI's import model as a bridge.
3. **What is your existing stack?** Heavy Microsoft investment is a real, legitimate reason to choose Power BI even if another tool scores higher in the abstract.
4. **What is your cost model tolerance?** Per-user (Power BI) is predictable. Consumption-linked tools (Sigma especially) require warehouse cost discipline.

## The mistake to avoid

The expensive error is buying a self-service tool to *avoid* building a semantic layer. ThoughtSpot and Sigma do not remove the need for a trustworthy model — they expose its absence to the entire company at once. We have watched a ThoughtSpot rollout get blamed for "wrong numbers" that were wrong in the warehouse all along; the tool just made it visible.

So the real prerequisite for the two self-service options is upstream:

- Agreed metric definitions in a semantic layer.
- A warehouse tuned for interactive query.
- Governance so users only see what they should.

## A defensible recommendation

If forced to a default: **Power BI** for organisations centred on Microsoft with a central BI function; **Sigma** for warehouse-native, spreadsheet-heavy analyst cultures; **ThoughtSpot** for organisations whose strategic goal is genuine self-service and who have done the modelling work to earn it. Pilot the shortlisted tool with *real* users on *real* questions for two weeks before signing. The demo always works; the pilot tells the truth.

posts.title: Data Governance and Security That People Actually Follow
posts.excerpt: Governance fails when it is a policy document nobody reads. Here is how to encode access, masking, and lineage as enforced platform features on Snowflake.
posts.body:
## Governance is code, not a PDF

The governance programmes that work share one trait: the rules are enforced by the platform, not by a wiki page people are supposed to have read. A policy that depends on humans remembering it is not a control — it is a hope. On a modern warehouse like Snowflake, almost every governance intent can be expressed as an enforced object.

## Start with a role model that maps to the org

The most common root cause of access chaos is a role hierarchy that grew organically. Reset it deliberately:

- **Functional roles** describe a job: `analyst_finance`, `engineer_data`, `analyst_marketing`.
- **Access roles** describe a permission on objects: `read_finance_schema`, `write_raw_schema`.
- Functional roles are *granted* access roles. Users are granted functional roles. Never grant object privileges directly to a user.

This two-layer pattern means onboarding a new finance analyst is one grant, and you can audit "who can read finance data" by inspecting one role.

## Mask at the column, not in the query

Sensitive columns should be protected by policy so that protection cannot be forgotten in an ad-hoc query. Dynamic masking does exactly this:

```sql
CREATE MASKING POLICY mask_email AS (val string) RETURNS string ->
  CASE
    WHEN CURRENT_ROLE() IN ('ANALYST_PII', 'ENGINEER_DATA') THEN val
    ELSE REGEXP_REPLACE(val, '.+@', '****@')
  END;

ALTER TABLE customers MODIFY COLUMN email
  SET MASKING POLICY mask_email;
```

Now every query against `customers.email` is masked unless the caller holds a privileged role — in dashboards, notebooks, and ad-hoc SQL alike. There is no path around it.

## Row access policies for multi-tenant and regional rules

Where different users should see different *rows* — a regional manager seeing only their region, or a SaaS product isolating tenants — use row access policies rather than filtering in every report:

```sql
CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY region_policy AS (region string)
  RETURNS boolean ->
    EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM entitlements e
      WHERE e.snowflake_role = CURRENT_ROLE()
        AND e.region = region
    );
```

The filter lives once, in the platform, and applies everywhere the table is touched. This matters across the Americas where data-residency and regional access rules differ by jurisdiction.

## Tag-based governance scales better than per-object rules

Managing masking policies object by object collapses under its own weight at a few hundred tables. Tags solve this. Classify columns once, attach policy to the tag, and any column carrying that tag inherits the control automatically — including columns created next month.

- Define tags: `pii`, `phi`, `financial`, `confidential`.
- Attach a masking policy to the tag, not the column.
- Use automatic classification to find candidate sensitive columns, then confirm and tag.

## Prove it: lineage and audit

Governance you cannot demonstrate is governance you do not have. Two questions every auditor and most CISOs eventually ask:

- **Where did this number come from?** Answered by lineage — column-level if you can. Snowflake's access history and a tool like dbt's lineage graph together give you source-to-report traceability.
- **Who saw this sensitive data, and when?** Answered by `ACCESS_HISTORY`:

```sql
SELECT user_name, query_start_time, direct_objects_accessed
FROM snowflake.account_usage.access_history
WHERE ARRAY_CONTAINS('MY_DB.HR.SALARIES'::variant,
        direct_objects_accessed)
  AND query_start_time >= DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_DATE());
```

## Make the secure path the easy path

The deepest principle in governance: people route around friction. If the governed dataset is slow and awkward and the ungoverned copy is fast, you will get an ungoverned copy on someone's laptop. So:

- Make the governed semantic layer the *fastest* way to get an answer.
- Grant access quickly through self-service requests with approval, not week-long tickets.
- Default to read access on non-sensitive data; reserve friction for genuinely sensitive assets.

## A governance baseline checklist

For a new Snowflake estate, day-one minimum:

- Two-layer role hierarchy, no direct user grants.
- Masking policies on all PII/PHI columns, attached via tags.
- Row access policies for any regional or tenant isolation.
- Access history retention and a scheduled review of privileged-role usage.
- A named owner for every database and schema.

Governance done this way is not a tax on velocity. It is what lets you say yes to the AI and self-service projects later without a six-week security review each time, because the controls are already proven and enforced in the platform.

posts.title: Agentic AI in the Enterprise: Past the Demo, Into Production
posts.excerpt: Agents that take actions are compelling in a demo and dangerous in production without the right scaffolding. Here is how to deploy them so they help rather than hallucinate their way into your systems.
posts.body:
## What an agent actually is

Strip away the marketing and an agent is a loop: a model that, given a goal, decides which tool to call, observes the result, and decides what to do next — repeating until it judges the goal met. The difference from a chatbot is that an agent *acts*. It queries databases, calls APIs, writes records. That capability is exactly what makes it useful and exactly what makes it risky.

## Why demos lie

An agent demo works because the demo-builder has implicitly bounded the problem. There is one happy path, the tools are mocked or forgiving, and a human is watching. Production has none of those. The agent will encounter ambiguous goals, tools that fail halfway, and inputs designed to manipulate it. The gap between "works in the demo" and "safe in production" is the entire engineering effort.

## The four things every production agent needs

### 1. Bounded, well-described tools

An agent is only as safe as the tools you give it. Each tool should:

- Do **one** thing, with a precise description the model can reason about.
- Validate its own inputs — never trust the model to format an argument correctly.
- Be **least-privilege**: a tool that reads orders cannot also delete them.
- Be **idempotent** where possible, so a retry does not double-charge a customer.

```python
def refund_order(order_id: str, amount_cents: int) -> dict:
    order = db.get_order(order_id)          # validate existence
    if order is None:
        return {"error": "order_not_found"}
    if amount_cents > order.refundable_cents:  # enforce business rule
        return {"error": "amount_exceeds_refundable"}
    return payments.refund(order_id, amount_cents, idempotency_key=order_id)
```

The business rules live in the tool, not in the prompt. A prompt is a suggestion; code is a guarantee.

### 2. A human in the loop for consequential actions

Classify actions by reversibility and blast radius. Reads and reversible writes can run autonomously. Irreversible or high-value actions — issuing a large refund, sending an external email, modifying production config — should require human confirmation. The agent proposes; a person approves. This single design choice prevents most catastrophic agent failures.

### 3. Observability and a stop button

You must be able to see what the agent did and halt it. At minimum, log every step: the model's reasoning, the tool called, the arguments, the result. Set hard limits — maximum steps per task, maximum spend per run, a timeout. An agent stuck in a loop calling an API 4,000 times is a real failure mode, not a hypothetical.

### 4. Evaluation against real scenarios

Before production, run the agent against a suite of realistic tasks — including adversarial and edge cases — and measure success, not vibes. Did it complete the task? Did it stay within bounds? Did it call the right tools? Re-run this suite on every prompt or model change, because both drift.

## A sane architecture

The pattern we deploy most often:

- A **planner** model that decomposes the goal into steps.
- A constrained set of **tools** with validation and least-privilege access.
- A **policy layer** that intercepts tool calls and enforces approval rules before execution.
- A **memory store** scoped to the task, not a global free-for-all.
- **Structured logging** of every step to your warehouse for audit and evaluation.

Notice the policy layer sits *between* the model and the tools. The model never calls a tool directly; it requests a call, and deterministic code decides whether to permit it. That inversion of control is what makes the system auditable.

## Where agents are worth it today

Be selective. Good early candidates share these traits: repetitive multi-step workflows, tolerance for a human checkpoint, and clear success criteria.

- **Internal ops** — triaging tickets, drafting responses, gathering context across systems for a human to approve.
- **Data workflows** — an agent that investigates a failed pipeline, gathers logs, and proposes a fix.
- **Research and synthesis** — pulling from multiple internal sources into a structured brief.

Where we counsel patience: anything touching money or external customers without a human checkpoint, and anything where a wrong action is hard to reverse.

## The honest assessment

Agentic AI is real and it is improving fast, but the organisations getting value from it are not the ones with the cleverest prompts. They are the ones who treated the agent as a junior employee with system access — given narrow permissions, supervised on consequential decisions, fully logged, and evaluated before promotion. Build the scaffolding first. The intelligence is the easy part now; the safety is the work.

posts.title: Embedded Analytics as a Product, Not a Feature
posts.excerpt: Bolting a dashboard into your app is easy. Building analytics your customers will pay for — and that scales to thousands of tenants — is a product discipline. Here is the difference.
posts.body:
## The feature trap

Many SaaS companies add analytics as a checkbox: embed an iframe, ship a few charts, call it "Insights." Customers glance at it once and never return. Meanwhile a competitor builds analytics that customers *log in specifically to use* — and charges for it. The difference is not the charting library. It is treating analytics as a product with its own users, roadmap, and economics.

## Three questions before you build

### Who is the user, and what decision do they make?

"Customers want reporting" is not a requirement. *Which* customer role, making *which* decision, at *what* moment? A warehouse manager deciding tomorrow's staffing needs a different surface than a CFO reviewing quarterly margin. Embedded analytics that tries to serve everyone serves no one. Pick the highest-value decision and design backward from it.

### Will they pay for it, or does it reduce churn?

Embedded analytics monetises two ways: as a paid tier (customers upgrade for deeper insight) or as retention (analytics makes your product stickier so customers stay). Decide which *before* building, because it changes what you build. A paid tier needs differentiated depth; a retention play needs frictionless ubiquity.

### How many tenants, and how isolated must they be?

This is the architectural fork. Ten enterprise tenants is a different system than ten thousand SMB tenants. Per-tenant isolation requirements — especially in regulated industries — drive your whole data model.

## The multi-tenant data architecture

The core challenge of embedded analytics is showing each customer *only their own data*, fast, at scale. On Snowflake, the patterns:

- **Single table, row-level isolation.** All tenants share tables; a row access policy keyed on the tenant filters every query. Best for many small tenants. The policy is the security boundary, so it must be airtight.
- **Schema or database per tenant.** Stronger isolation, easier to give a tenant their own data, but management overhead grows with tenant count. Best for fewer, larger, regulated tenants.
- **Hybrid.** Shared tables for the SMB long tail, dedicated schemas for enterprise accounts that demand isolation.

```sql
CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY tenant_isolation AS (tenant_id string)
  RETURNS boolean ->
    tenant_id = INVOKER_SHARE() OR
    tenant_id = CURRENT_ACCOUNT();
-- In practice the tenant id is injected via a session variable
-- set from the authenticated app context, never from user input.
```

The critical rule: the tenant identifier comes from your authenticated application session, never from a parameter the client controls. A tenant who can change their own tenant id can read everyone's data.

## Performance is the product

In embedded analytics, latency *is* the user experience. A dashboard that takes eight seconds to load is a dashboard nobody uses. Tactics that matter at tenant scale:

- **Pre-aggregate** the common rollups; do not recompute them per page load.
- Use **materialised views or scheduled tables** for the heavy, shared computations.
- **Cache** results per tenant with sensible invalidation.
- Right-size the **warehouse** and consider a dedicated warehouse for the embedded workload so a heavy internal query does not starve customer-facing dashboards.

## The economics you must model

The trap that sinks embedded analytics businesses: charging a flat fee while incurring per-query warehouse cost. A power-user tenant can quietly cost more than they pay. Before launch, model:

- Cost per tenant per month at the warehouse layer.
- The relationship between a tenant's usage and your cost.
- A pricing model that stays profitable for your heaviest users, not just your average.

Snowflake's per-second billing and the ability to attribute cost by warehouse make this measurable — instrument it from day one rather than discovering the unit economics after a heavy user signs up.

## Build vs embed vs partner

Three paths to the surface itself:

- **Embed a tool** (Sigma, ThoughtSpot, and others offer strong embedding) — fastest to market, less control over the exact UX.
- **Build custom** on a charting library against your warehouse via a semantic API — full control, much more engineering.
- **Hybrid** — embed for breadth, build custom for the two or three hero views that differentiate you.

For most teams, embedding to launch and selectively building the differentiated views is the right sequence.

## The product disciplines that separate winners

- **A roadmap and an owner.** Analytics is a product, so it gets a product manager, not a backlog ticket.
- **Usage instrumentation.** Track which charts customers actually use; kill the ones they ignore.
- **A semantic layer** so metrics mean the same thing in the embedded product as in your internal reporting.
- **Self-serve depth** so customers can answer follow-up questions without filing a support request.

Embedded analytics done as a feature is a cost centre. Done as a product, it is a revenue line and a retention moat. The technology is the same; the discipline is not.

posts.title: Snowflake Cost Optimisation: Where the Money Actually Goes
posts.excerpt: Snowflake bills are not mysterious — they are just under-instrumented. A systematic walkthrough of where credits disappear and the changes that recover them fast.
posts.body:
## The bill is a behaviour problem

Snowflake cost surprises are almost never the pricing model's fault. They are the predictable result of elastic compute meeting habits formed on fixed-capacity systems. The good news: because every credit is attributable, optimisation is an engineering exercise with measurable results, not a negotiation with a vendor. Most engagements recover 20-40% of spend in the first month without touching a single workload's outcome.

## First, see where the money goes

You cannot optimise what you cannot attribute. Start here:

```sql
SELECT warehouse_name,
       SUM(credits_used) AS credits,
       SUM(credits_used) * 3 AS approx_usd  -- adjust to your rate
FROM snowflake.account_usage.warehouse_metering_history
WHERE start_time >= DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_DATE())
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
```

Nine times out of ten, two or three warehouses dominate the bill. Optimisation effort goes there, not everywhere. The 80/20 is real.

## The big four cost drivers

### 1. Warehouses that never sleep

The single most common waste: a warehouse with auto-suspend set to 10 minutes (or disabled) sitting idle between queries, billing the whole time. Snowflake bills per second with a 60-second minimum per resume. Set **auto-suspend to 60 seconds** for most interactive warehouses. The trade-off is occasional cache warm-up; for the vast majority of workloads that is far cheaper than idle time.

```sql
ALTER WAREHOUSE analytics_wh SET
  AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
  AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;
```

### 2. Oversized warehouses

Teams size warehouses for the worst query and then run everything on that size. A query that runs in 4 seconds on a Large and 3.5 seconds on an XL is wasting money on the XL — you doubled the credits-per-second for a 12% gain. Right-sizing rule: increase size only when a query is *spilling to disk* or queueing. Check spillage:

```sql
SELECT query_id, warehouse_size,
       bytes_spilled_to_local_storage,
       bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage
FROM snowflake.account_usage.query_history
WHERE bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage > 0
  AND start_time >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_DATE())
ORDER BY bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

Remote spillage is the signal to size up. Its absence on a large warehouse is the signal to size down.

### 3. Inefficient queries scanning everything

Snowflake prunes partitions using clustering. Queries that filter on a column the table is not organised by scan the whole table. Symptoms: high `partitions_scanned` relative to `partitions_total`. Fixes:

- Filter on the natural ordering column (often a date) where possible.
- For large, frequently-filtered tables, consider a **clustering key** on the common filter column — but only after measuring; clustering has its own maintenance cost.
- Avoid `SELECT *` in transformations; column pruning is free savings.

### 4. Workload mixing

When ad-hoc analyst queries, scheduled ELT, and a BI tool all share one warehouse, they queue behind each other and you size up to compensate — paying premium size for everything. Separate workloads onto right-sized warehouses. Use **multi-cluster** warehouses for spiky concurrent workloads (it scales out then back in) rather than a permanently oversized single cluster.

## The controls that prevent the next surprise

Optimisation is not a one-off. Install guardrails:

- **Resource monitors** with alerts and hard suspend thresholds per warehouse. This is your circuit breaker against a runaway backfill.
- **Statement timeouts** so a pathological query cannot run for six hours.
- **A cost-attribution model** — tag warehouses by team or product so cost has an owner. Untagged cost is unaccountable cost.
- **A weekly review** of the top warehouses and most expensive queries for the first few months.

## Storage and the quiet costs

Compute dominates, but do not ignore:

- **Time Travel and Fail-safe** retention on huge transient tables — set retention appropriately rather than the maximum everywhere.
- **Cortex and serverless features** — these bill separately; include them in attribution.
- **Cloned environments** left running — dev clones that nobody suspends.

## A pragmatic optimisation sprint

For a team facing a bill that has crept up, a two-week sprint that reliably delivers:

1. Attribute spend by warehouse and identify the top three.
2. Set auto-suspend to 60s everywhere it is not already.
3. Right-size based on spillage evidence, not intuition.
4. Separate the worst workload-mixing offender onto its own warehouse.
5. Find the ten most expensive queries and fix the pruning on the worst.
6. Install resource monitors and tagging so it does not regress.

Done properly, the result is a bill that is lower, predictable, and — most importantly — attributable, so the next person who asks "why did the bill go up" gets an answer in minutes instead of a shrug.

posts.title: Data Engineering That Holds Up: ELT, dbt, and Matillion in Practice
posts.excerpt: The patterns that separate a pipeline you can sleep through from one that pages you at 3am. Opinionated guidance on layering, testing, and tooling for modern ELT.
posts.body:
## ELT won, and it changed the discipline

The shift from ETL to ELT — load raw data first, transform inside the warehouse — is not just a reordering of letters. It changes where your logic lives, how you test it, and who can contribute. Transformations become version-controlled SQL instead of opaque jobs in a proprietary GUI. That single change is what makes data engineering look like software engineering. The practices below follow from taking that seriously.

## Layer your transformations deliberately

The most common cause of an unmaintainable warehouse is transformation logic with no architecture — a tangle where any model can reference any other. Impose layers:

- **Staging (`stg_`)** — one model per source table. Light cleaning only: rename columns to a standard, cast types, no joins, no business logic. This is your insulation layer; if a source changes, you fix it here once.
- **Intermediate (`int_`)** — the joins and reshaping that are too complex to inline but are not yet a business concept. Ephemeral where possible.
- **Marts (`fct_`, `dim_`)** — the business-facing models. A `fct_orders`, a `dim_customer`. These are what analysts and BI tools consume.

The rule that makes this work: **dependencies only flow downward.** Staging never references marts. A mart never references another mart's internals, only its outputs. Enforce it in review.

## Test like the data will betray you

Untested pipelines fail silently — the worst kind of failure, because someone makes a decision on wrong numbers before anyone notices. In dbt, tests are cheap and should be everywhere that matters:

```yaml
models:
  - name: fct_orders
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: customer_id
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('dim_customer')
              field: customer_id
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled']
```

Beyond the built-ins, add tests that encode *business* invariants: revenue is never negative, a delivered order has a delivery date, daily row counts stay within an expected band. These catch the bugs that schema tests miss.

## Make models idempotent and incremental — correctly

A model should produce the same result whether run once or ten times. For large tables, incremental models avoid reprocessing history — but incremental logic is where subtle bugs breed. The discipline:

- Define a clear **unique key** so re-runs update rather than duplicate.
- Handle **late-arriving data** with a lookback window, not just `where updated_at > max(updated_at)`.
- Keep a **full-refresh path** that you actually test, because you will need it.

## dbt and Matillion: not a rivalry

Teams ask which to choose as if it is either/or. They solve different problems.

- **Matillion** excels at **orchestration and ingestion** — pulling from dozens of sources, handling API pagination, managing complex job dependencies with a visual interface that a broader team can maintain. It is strong where you need to *get data in* and coordinate jobs.
- **dbt** excels at **transformation as code** — testable, version-controlled, documented SQL with lineage. It is strong once data is *in* the warehouse.

A common, sound architecture: Matillion (or another ingestion tool) lands raw data and orchestrates the schedule; dbt owns the transformation logic from raw to marts. Use each for its strength rather than forcing one to do the other's job. Where a team is small and SQL-native, dbt plus a lightweight scheduler may be all you need; where ingestion is the hard part, Matillion earns its place.

## The operational practices that prevent 3am

Good pipelines are boring because of process, not luck:

- **CI on every change.** Build and test the affected models in a temporary schema before merge. A broken model never reaches production.
- **Environment separation.** Dev, staging, prod with separate targets. Engineers build against dev data, not prod.
- **Freshness checks.** Alert when a source has not updated when expected — a stale source is a silent failure.
- **Documentation as a byproduct.** dbt generates docs and lineage from the code itself. A model without a description fails review.
- **Ownership.** Every mart has a named owner. Orphaned models are how warehouses rot.

## What "done" looks like for a model

Before a transformation merges, it should have: a clear layer assignment, a unique-key test, not-null tests on keys, relationship tests to its dimensions, at least one business-invariant test, a description on the model and its key columns, and a passing CI run. That checklist feels heavy the first week and saves you every week after.

## The throughline

Every practice here borrows from software engineering: version control, testing, CI, code review, modular architecture, ownership. The teams whose pipelines are calm are the ones who stopped treating data work as scripting and started treating it as engineering. The tools — dbt, Matillion, Snowflake — are good, but they reward discipline and punish its absence.

posts.title: The Semantic Layer: One Definition of Revenue, Finally
posts.excerpt: Why your three dashboards disagree about revenue, and how a semantic layer ends the argument by defining metrics once, in code, for every tool that asks.
posts.body:
## The meeting where the numbers do not match

Every data leader has been in this meeting. Sales shows revenue of 4.2 million. Finance shows 3.9. Both are "right" — they used different definitions of revenue, baked into different dashboards by different people at different times. The next hour is spent not deciding anything, but reconciling. Multiply that by every metric and every meeting, and you have quantified the cost of not having a semantic layer.

## What a semantic layer is

A semantic layer is a single, governed definition of your business metrics and dimensions, sitting between the physical warehouse tables and the tools that consume them. It answers "what is revenue" once, in one place, and every BI tool, notebook, and AI assistant gets the same answer. The physical tables stay as they are; the semantic layer maps business concepts onto them.

Concretely it defines:

- **Metrics** — revenue, active users, gross margin — with their exact calculation.
- **Dimensions** — the ways you slice metrics: by region, product, time, segment.
- **Relationships** — how the underlying tables join, so consumers do not re-derive joins.
- **Grain and filters** — what a row means and which records count.

## Why it is worth the effort

- **One source of truth.** Revenue is defined once. The Sales-vs-Finance meeting stops happening.
- **Tool independence.** Switch BI tools, add an AI assistant, build an embedded product — the metric definitions come along. You are not re-implementing logic per tool.
- **Governance.** Definitions are reviewed, version-controlled, and auditable. A change to "revenue" is a pull request, not a quiet edit in a dashboard.
- **AI readiness.** This is the unlock for natural-language analytics. Tools like Snowflake's Cortex Analyst and ThoughtSpot only give trustworthy answers when they query a defined semantic model rather than guessing at raw tables.

## What a definition looks like

In a dbt semantic model, a metric is declarative:

```yaml
semantic_models:
  - name: orders
    model: ref('fct_orders')
    entities:
      - name: order_id
        type: primary
    dimensions:
      - name: order_date
        type: time
        type_params: {time_granularity: day}
      - name: region
        type: categorical
    measures:
      - name: net_revenue
        agg: sum
        expr: amount - discount - refunds

metrics:
  - name: net_revenue
    type: simple
    type_params:
      measure: net_revenue
```

Now `net_revenue` means `amount - discount - refunds`, aggregated by sum, everywhere. A query for net revenue by region by month is a request against this model, not a hand-written join an analyst might get subtly wrong.

## The hard part is not technical

Building the semantic layer in a tool takes days. Getting the organisation to *agree on the definitions* takes the real work. "What counts as an active user" is a business decision with stakeholders who hold different, reasonable views. The semantic layer forces those disagreements into the open and resolves them once. That is uncomfortable and it is the entire value — you are converting implicit, conflicting assumptions into an explicit, single decision.

A process that works:

- Inventory the metrics currently in use and document every definition in the wild. You will find the same metric defined three ways.
- Convene the owners — finance, sales, product — and force a decision on each contested metric.
- Encode the agreed definition in the semantic layer.
- Deprecate the divergent versions and migrate consumers.

## Where it lives in your stack

The semantic layer sits above your transformation layer. dbt builds clean marts; the semantic layer defines metrics on top of those marts; BI tools, the AI assistant, and embedded products consume the metrics through a consistent interface. Some platforms (Snowflake's semantic views, dbt's semantic layer, and others) offer the layer natively; the principle matters more than the specific tool.

## Start small, prove value

Do not try to model every metric on day one. Pick the three to five metrics that show up in the most meetings and cause the most arguments. Define those, point your primary BI tool at them, and demonstrate that two teams now get the same number. That proof — the same revenue figure in two places, derived from one definition — is what earns the mandate to do the rest.

The semantic layer is not glamorous. It is plumbing. But it is the plumbing that decides whether your AI answers are trustworthy, your BI migration is painless, and your leadership meetings are about decisions instead of reconciliation.

posts.title: RAG on Your Warehouse: Grounding LLMs in Data You Trust
posts.excerpt: Retrieval-augmented generation stops a model inventing answers by feeding it your real documents. Here is how to build it on Snowflake without standing up a separate vector-database empire.
posts.body:
## The problem RAG solves

Ask a general-purpose LLM about your company's refund policy and it will answer confidently — and wrong, because it has never seen your policy. Retrieval-augmented generation fixes this by retrieving the relevant passages from *your* documents and giving them to the model as context, instructing it to answer only from what it is shown. The model becomes a reasoning and phrasing engine over your trusted content rather than a source of facts itself.

## The architecture, honestly

RAG is four steps, and each can be done well or badly:

1. **Chunk** your documents into passages.
2. **Embed** each chunk into a vector and store it.
3. **Retrieve** the chunks most relevant to a user's question.
4. **Generate** an answer from the retrieved chunks, with the model instructed to cite or stay grounded.

The common mistake is treating this as solely a model problem. In practice, retrieval quality dominates answer quality. If you retrieve the wrong chunks, the best model in the world produces a confident wrong answer.

## Why build it on the warehouse

The instinct is to spin up a dedicated vector database. For many organisations — especially those whose source content already lives near the warehouse and who care about governance — building RAG inside Snowflake is simpler and more governable. Embeddings, vector storage, vector search, and generation all live in one place, inheriting your existing access controls and audit trail. No separate system to secure, no data copied out to a third party.

Snowflake provides the pieces natively: embedding functions, a `VECTOR` data type, vector distance functions, and Cortex Search as a managed retrieval service.

## Building it

Start by embedding your chunks. Assume you have already chunked documents into a `doc_chunks` table:

```sql
ALTER TABLE doc_chunks ADD COLUMN embedding VECTOR(FLOAT, 768);

UPDATE doc_chunks
SET embedding = AI_EMBED('snowflake-arctic-embed-m', chunk_text);
```

Retrieval is a vector similarity search:

```sql
SELECT chunk_text,
       VECTOR_COSINE_SIMILARITY(
         embedding,
         AI_EMBED('snowflake-arctic-embed-m', ?)  -- user question
       ) AS score
FROM doc_chunks
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Then generation grounds the model in those chunks:

```sql
SELECT AI_COMPLETE(
  'claude-sonnet',
  CONCAT(
    'Answer using ONLY the context below. If the answer is not in ',
    'the context, say you do not know.\n\nContext:\n', :context,
    '\n\nQuestion: ', :question
  )
);
```

For production you would typically use Cortex Search, which manages the indexing and retrieval and combines vector with keyword search — but the principle is the SQL above.

## The details that decide whether it works

### Chunking is not an afterthought

Chunk too large and retrieval pulls in irrelevant text that dilutes the answer; too small and you lose context. Chunk on semantic boundaries — sections, paragraphs — not arbitrary character counts. Overlap chunks slightly so a concept split across a boundary is not lost. Keep metadata (document, section, date) with each chunk so you can filter and cite.

### Hybrid retrieval beats pure vector

Vector search is great at semantic similarity but can miss exact terms — product codes, names, acronyms. Combining vector search with keyword search (which Cortex Search does) catches both. A question containing a specific SKU should retrieve the chunk with that SKU even if it is not semantically "similar."

### Filter before you retrieve

If a question is about 2026 policy, do not retrieve 2019 chunks. Use metadata filters — date, department, document type — to constrain the search space before similarity ranking. This single practice fixes a large share of "it gave me an outdated answer" complaints.

### Always cite, and let it say "I do not know"

Two non-negotiable behaviours: the system should show *which* source each answer came from so users can verify, and the prompt must permit "I do not know" when retrieval finds nothing relevant. A RAG system that always answers is a RAG system that lies when it should abstain.

## Evaluating it

Do not ship on vibes. Build an evaluation set of real questions with known correct answers and measure:

- **Retrieval recall** — did the right chunk make it into the context? If not, no fix downstream helps.
- **Answer faithfulness** — does the answer stick to the retrieved context, or does it hallucinate?
- **Refusal correctness** — does it correctly say "I do not know" when the answer is genuinely absent?

Re-run this on every change to chunking, the embedding model, or the prompt.

## The governance dividend

Because the whole pipeline lives in the warehouse, your existing controls apply. A user asking the RAG system a question only retrieves chunks from documents they are permitted to see — enforced by the same row access policies governing everything else. For regulated clients, this means a RAG deployment does not require a separate security review of a new data store; it inherits the one you already passed. That is often the deciding factor in getting RAG into production rather than leaving it in a sandbox.

posts.title: The Data Team Operating Model: Centralised, Embedded, or Mesh?
posts.excerpt: How you organise a data team shapes everything it can deliver. A clear-eyed comparison of the three dominant models and how to choose — or evolve between — them.
posts.body:
## Org design is a technical decision

Leaders treat data-team structure as an HR matter and data architecture as a technical one. They are the same decision. A centralised team builds a centralised platform; an embedded model produces domain-shaped data products; a mesh demands platform investment most companies underestimate. Choose the operating model deliberately, because your architecture will conform to it whether you intend it to or not.

## The three models

### Centralised

A single data team owns the platform, the pipelines, and the analytics. Business units file requests; the team prioritises and delivers.

- **Strengths:** consistency, strong governance, no duplicated effort, a clear home for scarce expertise, easy to maintain standards.
- **Weaknesses:** becomes a bottleneck as demand grows; the central team lacks deep domain context; business units feel un-served and build shadow data ops in spreadsheets.
- **Best when:** the organisation is small-to-mid, or early in its data maturity, or governance is paramount (regulated industries).

### Embedded (decentralised)

Data professionals sit *within* business units — analytics engineers in finance, in marketing, in operations — close to the domain and its decisions.

- **Strengths:** deep domain context, fast turnaround, business units feel ownership, work is prioritised by the people who feel the pain.
- **Weaknesses:** inconsistency across units, duplicated pipelines, governance drift, the same metric defined five ways, career isolation for the embedded individuals.
- **Best when:** domains are genuinely different, the business moves fast, and you have *some* central function holding standards.

### Data mesh

Domains own their data as *products*, served over a shared self-service platform built by a central platform team, governed by federated standards.

- **Strengths:** scales to large, complex organisations; domain ownership with consistency; the platform team enables rather than bottlenecks.
- **Weaknesses:** demands serious platform investment and organisational maturity; done prematurely it is just decentralisation with a fashionable name and worse governance.
- **Best when:** you are large, you have many domains, and you have already built a credible self-service platform. Not before.

## The hybrid most teams actually run

In practice the durable answer for mid-to-large organisations is a **hub-and-spoke** model:

- A **central platform/governance team** owns the warehouse, the ingestion framework, the semantic layer, security, and standards. It builds the paved road.
- **Embedded analytics engineers** in domains build on that road, close to the business, owning their domain's marts and dashboards.
- A **community of practice** connects the embedded individuals so they share patterns and do not drift into isolation.

This captures domain speed without sacrificing consistency, provided the central team genuinely *enables* rather than *controls*. The failure mode is a central team that becomes a gatekeeper; then the spokes route around it and you are back to shadow IT.

## How to choose

Answer these honestly:

- **What is your data maturity?** Low maturity → centralise first. You cannot federate governance you have never had.
- **How different are your domains?** Very different → favour embedding. Similar → centralised efficiency wins.
- **How big is the demand backlog?** A central team drowning in requests is a signal to embed.
- **Have you built a self-service platform?** No → you are not ready for mesh, regardless of how appealing the diagram looks.

## Evolution, not religion

The right model changes as the organisation grows. A healthy trajectory:

1. **Start centralised** to establish the platform, governance, and standards while maturity is low.
2. **Embed selectively** into the highest-demand domains as the backlog grows, keeping the central team as the standards owner.
3. **Move toward mesh** only once the self-service platform is real and multiple domains can genuinely own products on it.

Most organisations get into trouble by skipping to step three because it is fashionable, or by clinging to step one long after the central team has become the bottleneck strangling the business.

## The roles that make any model work

Whatever the structure, certain functions must exist and be owned:

- **Platform** — the warehouse, ingestion, and self-service tooling.
- **Governance** — definitions, access, lineage, standards.
- **Analytics engineering** — turning raw data into trustworthy marts.
- **Analytics/BI** — turning marts into decisions.
- **Product** — especially if data is an external product.

In a centralised model one team holds all of these; in a mesh they are distributed. What never works is leaving any of them unowned. The operating model is ultimately about making ownership explicit — and the cost of ambiguous ownership is the shadow spreadsheets, the conflicting numbers, and the AI projects that never reach production.

studies.challenge:
Northwind Bank, a mid-tier North American retail and commercial lender, was running its enterprise data warehouse on an ageing on-premises appliance that had reached end-of-life support. Regulatory reporting — including liquidity coverage, credit-risk exposure, and BSA/AML transaction monitoring — depended on overnight batch jobs that routinely overran their windows, leaving risk and finance teams waiting until mid-morning for figures that should have been ready at open.

Data was siloed across the core banking platform, a separate cards system, and a patchwork of departmental marts. Reconciliation between these sources was manual and error-prone, and every new regulatory request triggered weeks of bespoke ETL work. Capacity contention was acute: a heavy risk-aggregation run could starve the analysts producing branch performance dashboards, forcing the bank to throttle reporting during peak periods.

Leadership wanted a governed, auditable platform that could scale elastically, satisfy examiners on data lineage and access controls, and give risk, finance, and the lines of business a single trusted version of the numbers — without the capital expense and refresh cycle of another appliance.
studies.solution:
Viewnear designed and delivered a Snowflake-based enterprise data warehouse organised around a layered medallion architecture: raw landing zones per source system, a conformed integration layer modelled on a banking-specific data vault, and curated presentation marts for risk, finance, and retail reporting. Snowpipe and a Kafka connector ingested core banking and cards transactions in near real time, while batch extracts from legacy systems landed via secured external stages.

We separated workloads using dedicated virtual warehouses — one for heavy risk and regulatory aggregation, others for finance close and BI — so that no team's queries could degrade another's. Multi-cluster scaling absorbed month-end and quarter-end spikes automatically. Sensitive fields such as account numbers and PII were protected with dynamic data masking and row-access policies, and every transformation was version-controlled in dbt with full lineage captured for examiners.

For regulatory reporting we built parameterised, schedule-driven pipelines that produced the liquidity, credit-exposure, and transaction-monitoring extracts on a fixed SLA, with automated reconciliation checks between source and warehouse balances. Time Travel and zero-copy cloning gave the team safe, instant environments for testing new report logic against production data without duplicating storage.
studies.results:
Regulatory and risk reporting that previously landed mid-morning now completes well before market open, with the overnight batch window cut by more than half and reconciliation breaks flagged automatically rather than discovered by hand. Examiners praised the end-to-end lineage and policy-driven access controls during the bank's next supervisory review.

Because workloads are isolated and storage is decoupled from compute, the bank eliminated the contention that used to force reporting throttling, and it retired the on-premises appliance along with its maintenance and refresh costs. New regulatory requests that once took weeks of custom ETL are now delivered in days using the conformed integration layer.

The platform has become the bank's single source of truth: risk, finance, and the retail business now reconcile to the same governed figures, and the data team spends its time building new analytics rather than nursing overnight jobs.

quote.text: For the first time our risk and finance teams open the day looking at the same trusted numbers. Viewnear didn't just lift and shift our warehouse — they gave our examiners the lineage and controls they'd been asking for, and they gave us back our mornings.
quote.author: Margaret Colson

studies.challenge:
AndesPay, a fast-growing digital payments provider operating across several LATAM markets, was processing millions of transactions daily but had no unified view of them. Each market ran its own operational database, settlement records lived in spreadsheets and vendor portals, and the analytics team stitched together reports by exporting CSVs and merging them by hand — a process that broke whenever a country added a new acquirer or currency.

The finance team could not close monthly settlement reconciliation on time, and disputes with banking partners over interchange and fees dragged on because there was no authoritative transaction ledger to point to. Meanwhile, the fraud and risk team lacked a consolidated dataset to spot cross-border patterns, and product managers were flying blind on funnel and authorisation-rate metrics by market.

AndesPay needed a central enterprise data warehouse that could absorb multi-currency, multi-country transaction streams, reconcile settlements automatically, and serve clean, governed data to finance, risk, and product — all while meeting data-residency expectations across the region.
studies.solution:
Viewnear built AndesPay's enterprise data warehouse on Snowflake as the consolidation hub for every market. We implemented change-data-capture pipelines from each country's operational database into Snowflake, normalising disparate schemas into a single conformed transaction and settlement model. Currency conversion and fee logic were standardised in dbt transformations so that every market's data rolled up consistently to group-level reporting.

The core of the solution was an automated settlement reconciliation engine: incoming acquirer and bank settlement files were ingested via Snowpipe into staging, matched against the internal transaction ledger using configurable matching rules, and any exceptions were surfaced to a dedicated finance workflow. This replaced the manual CSV merging entirely and gave finance a defensible position in partner disputes.

We layered governed semantic models for three audiences — finance reconciliation, risk and fraud analytics, and product performance — each backed by role-based access and dynamic masking of cardholder data to keep the platform aligned with PCI expectations. Secure data sharing let trusted banking partners receive their reconciled extracts directly from Snowflake without ad-hoc file transfers.
studies.results:
Monthly settlement reconciliation that used to slip past deadline now closes on schedule, with the matching engine clearing the vast majority of records automatically and routing only genuine exceptions to analysts. Partner fee disputes are resolved faster because finance can cite an authoritative, reconciled ledger rather than reconstructing the numbers.

The risk team finally has a unified, cross-market dataset and has begun detecting fraud patterns that were invisible when each country sat in its own silo. Product managers now track authorisation rates and conversion funnels per market in self-service dashboards refreshed throughout the day.

As AndesPay expands into new markets, onboarding a country's data is now a configuration exercise on top of the conformed model rather than a fresh integration project — shortening the path from launch to full reporting coverage.

quote.text: We used to dread close week because reconciliation was a manual scramble across five countries. Now the matching runs itself and we walk into partner negotiations with one ledger everyone trusts. Viewnear built us a platform that grows as fast as we do.
quote.author: Diego Marroquín

studies.challenge:
Maple Retail, a Canadian grocery chain with several hundred stores, was losing significant margin to perishable shrink. Landing raw data with a Matillion load job
dbt project structure: staging, intermediate and mart layers

Adding dbt tests and documentation

labs.title: Power BI on Snowflake: DirectQuery, Import & Performance Tuning

DirectQuery vs Import vs composite models
Query folding and pushdown to Snowflake
Warehouse sizing and result caching for BI workloads
Managing concurrency and refresh cost

labs.title: Building a Semantic Layer with Snowflake Cortex Analyst

Authoring a Cortex Analyst semantic model (YAML)
Defining dimensions, measures and verified queries
Synonyms and business-friendly naming
Testing natural-language questions against the model

labs.title: RBAC & Governance: Role Hierarchies, Masking & Row Access Policies

Building a role hierarchy with grants and inheritance
Dynamic data masking policies on PII columns

Tag-based governance and the access history view

Creating resource monitors with alerts and suspend triggers
Attributing cost with query tags and warehouse separation
Spotting expensive queries and warehouse idle time
Auto-suspend, auto-resume and right-sizing strategies

labs.title: RAG & Vector Search: Build Retrieval-Augmented Answers with Cortex Search

VECTOR data type and vector similarity functions
Creating and querying a Cortex Search service
Assembling a RAG prompt with retrieved context
Evaluating relevance and reducing hallucination

news.excerpt: Announced at Snowflake Summit 2026 in San Francisco, Viewnear has been named the 2026 Snowflake Services Growth Partner of the Year for the Americas.
news.body:
Announced at Snowflake Summit 2026 in San Francisco, Viewnear has been named the **2026 Snowflake Services Growth Partner of the Year — Americas** by Snowflake, the AI Data Cloud company. The award recognises Viewnear's achievements within the Snowflake AI Data Cloud ecosystem, helping joint customers modernise their data platforms, accelerate AI adoption, and unlock faster, more actionable insights across Canada, the USA, Mexico, LATAM, and the Caribbean.

The recognition reflects a year of sustained delivery across financial services, healthcare, retail, and agriculture. Through deep expertise in Snowflake architecture, data engineering, and advanced analytics, Viewnear helps organisations operationalise data and AI at scale. Our pragmatic, business-first approach means clients don't just stand up a modern data foundation — they translate it into measurable outcomes: lower risk and cost, improved operational efficiency, and new revenue opportunities.

By combining Snowflake with leading ecosystem tools including Matillion, dbt, ThoughtSpot, Sigma, and Power BI, Viewnear delivers scalable, cloud-native data platforms that support real-world decision-making. The Growth Partner of the Year award is a measure of momentum — new clients won, platforms shipped to production, and AI use cases moved from proof of concept into daily operations — and it places Viewnear among the partners driving Snowflake adoption fastest across the region.

"This award belongs to our team and to the clients who trusted us to deliver," said Jordan Mendez, Director of Strategy & Partnerships at Viewnear. "In a data-driven market, the ability to synthesise, analyse, and operationalise insight is no longer optional — it is both an operational necessity and a strategic advantage. We're proud to work with organisations across the Americas who see that opportunity and choose Snowflake as the platform to realise it."

news.body:

It represents the pinnacle of Snowflake's partner programme — and it confirms Viewnear's position as a leading data and AI partner across the Americas.

Elite is not awarded on tenure. Organisations must meet the highest standards across every dimension of the partnership simultaneously: certified technical expertise, a proven record of complex and successful customer implementations, active contribution to the Snowflake ecosystem, and strong commercial performance. Reaching Elite means every part of the consulting practice — strategy, architecture, engineering, analytics, and AI — is operating at the highest level at the same time.

Viewnear's elevation is grounded in real client outcomes. Working with organisations across financial services, healthcare, retail, and agriculture in Canada, the USA, Mexico, LATAM, and the Caribbean, we have consistently delivered modern, cloud-native data platforms that reduce time to insight, sharpen decision-making, and lay the foundations for scalable AI adoption.
